newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh may buy power to boost investment.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh may buy power to boost investment.

text.p: Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina said on Tuesday her government was looking to buy electricity from other countries to ensure uninterrupted power supply and encourage investment.
"Investors want unhindered power supply and political stability to stake their money. But our energy sector is in shambles," she told a news conference.
"Energy must be given top priority for fast industrial development and overall economic progress. So we may go for buying electricity.
"We don't have any particular country in mind," Hasina said when a reporter asked if Bangladesh had already decided to procure power from neighbouring India.
"We want to buy it from who can provide it at a cheaper price and ensure quicker delivery."
The opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) led by former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia and several fringe parties have said they will resist any attempt to procure electricity from India.
"If they are saying so they should first stop consuming other Indian goods -- beef, rice, pulses, eggs, sugar and many other items," the prime minister said.

"The BNP government had opened the entire border for Indian goods to be smuggled into this country during its rule. We are trying to get something on a state-to- state basis, at competitive and respectable terms."
The prime minister said adequate supply of electricity could change the country's entire rural economic infrastructure and stop the influx of the poor into the cities.

Hasina described her recently concluded visit to China and Hong Kong as very fruitful. "We have urged China to invest more in Bangladesh and buy more goods from us. The response was very positive," she said without giving details.
" A large number of international investors we met in Hong Kong were very keen to invest in Bangladesh.
"I have explained to them that an investment climate already exists in our country and that the remaining hurdles would be removed through necessary reforms."
Hasina, who took over in June following her Awami League's victory in general elections, said she was determined to pursue free market economic policies and give "maximum priority to investment."

Direct foreign investment in Bangladesh totalled $915.6 million in the six months to December 1995 against $729.4 million in fiscal 1994/95 (July-June), according to the latest available official figures.

Hasina said she wanted to attract more investment at a faster pace through stronger ties with members of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), which groups Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.
